table.saw: The row beside the nominal report holds ONE box (Nominal report before T/O); there is no box for the words the button fills in. Labels containing word/text/rally/in-time/report: ["Nominal report before T/O"]. Setting keys on the page: step, dekit, briefLead, reportLead, debrief, minTurn, dur, openEnd, crewRest, tightTurn, longDay, maxRun, epBrief, simDebrief, amtDebrief, simLen, scDayFrom, scDayTo, inputLead, oilFullMin. Page lines mentioning the words setting: ["With one overlay (26 Aug 26): a personal-input commitment across the shift is graded by its TYPE — Training, CSE, Fly with, Personal, Appointment, Duty, Other are a Warning, because the shift may launch him; a Meeting stays an Advisory. A type the engine does not recognise — a typo, or a record from an older store — reads as the Warning too, never the advisory: when in doubt the engine assumes the serious case. A ground row carrying one of those words — lifted from an input or typed by hand — grades as the commitment it is, not as academics. A programme item always stays advisory.","The issued copy of a day is the squadron's word about what was worked, and it keeps crediting exactly what it credited — nothing moves on its own. But the men behind that puck earned nothing from that seat, because the app was not counting it when the day went out, and they should have. So the day raises the ordinary pending mark and waits for the scheduler to acknowledge it, which is what publishing again does. It says this in words rather than leaving a bare \"1 pending\" behind, because the copy that went out never wrote down who was behind the puck — so there is no cell to mark and nothing to show in History, and a scheduler would otherwise be republishing blind. One amendment per affected day, once.","The sortie itself measures nothing, so on the face of it nobody should earn from it. They do, and deliberately: a flying day runs from the report three hours before take-off to the debrief two hours after landing, and the crew did both. They were in squadron whatever the times say, which is the squadron's own fact rather than anything the times can show. So the line is never refused and no credit is taken away — the warning exists because a nought-minute sortie is always a slip of the keyboard, and it is cheaper to fix while the day is being built than after it has gone out. It names the line, not the crew: the times are the scheduler's to correct. A line that has no readable times at all is a different problem and carries the other warning — that one really does earn nobody anything. A standby SHIFT is the other way round: SC, AVALON and BB have no report and no debrief, so their window is the written window and one typed to the same minute earns nobody anything at all. The warning says so in those words on a shift, and the day names it — as a shift, not as a desk — in the same list as a desk with no usable times."]. Search "rally" shows rules: ["SETTING Each line uses its first recognised clock, such as 09:00H or 0900. Write IN TIME, RALLY, or both; an older clock-only instruction still means in-time. R","SETTING For a flight, a reporting clock later than take-off means the immediately previous day. The earliest applicable in-time or rally starts the crew's repor","WARNING REPORT_ORDER Present stages must run in-time → rally → brief → take-off → landing. Equal adjacent times are allowed. A reversed pair names the formation","ADVISORY REPORT_UNRESOLVED An unrecognised reporting clock, or RALLY AFTER IN TIME with no applicable in-time. The button's own fill on this build is always "<clock>H: IN TIME + WX/NOTAMS" (P2-08).

wordHits: With one overlay (26 Aug 26): a personal-input commitment across the shift is graded by its TYPE — Training, CSE, Fly with, Personal, Appointment, Duty, Other are a Warning, because the shift may launch him; a Meeting stays an Advisory. A type the engine does not recognise — a typo, or a record from an older store — reads as the Warning too, never the advisory: when in doubt the engine assumes the serious case. A ground row carrying one of those words — lifted from an input or typed by hand — grades as the commitment it is, not as academics. A programme item always stays advisory.

The issued copy of a day is the squadron's word about what was worked, and it keeps crediting exactly what it credited — nothing moves on its own. But the men behind that puck earned nothing from that seat, because the app was not counting it when the day went out, and they should have. So the day raises the ordinary pending mark and waits for the scheduler to acknowledge it, which is what publishing again does. It says this in words rather than leaving a bare "1 pending" behind, because the copy that went out never wrote down who was behind the puck — so there is no cell to mark and nothing to show in History, and a scheduler would otherwise be republishing blind. One amendment per affected day, once.

The sortie itself measures nothing, so on the face of it nobody should earn from it. They do, and deliberately: a flying day runs from the report three hours before take-off to the debrief two hours after landing, and the crew did both. They were in squadron whatever the times say, which is the squadron's own fact rather than anything the times can show. So the line is never refused and no credit is taken away — the warning exists because a nought-minute sortie is always a slip of the keyboard, and it is cheaper to fix while the day is being built than after it has gone out. It names the line, not the crew: the times are the scheduler's to correct. A line that has no readable times at all is a different problem and carries the other warning — that one really does earn nobody anything. A standby SHIFT is the other way round: SC, AVALON and BB have no report and no debrief, so their window is the written window and one typed to the same minute earns nobody anything at all. The warning says so in those words on a shift, and the day names it — as a shift, not as a desk — in the same list as a desk with no usable times.
